title: Classic Cheeseburger
summary: A no-nonsense beef cheeseburger with a deep seared crust, melted cheddar and all the classic fresh toppings, built for juice rather than fuss.
equipment: large heavy frying pan or cast-iron skillet (at least 26 cm)
lid or large upturned heatproof bowl

ingredients.item: soft burger buns or brioche-style buns
small red onion, thinly sliced into rings

steps.title: Shape the patties
steps.text: Divide 600g cold beef mince into four 150g portions and shape gently into patties 11-12cm wide and about 1.5cm thick, a little wider than the bun since they shrink as they cook. Press a shallow dimple into the centre of each with your thumb so they cook flat instead of doming. Handling the mince as little as possible keeps the texture tender rather than dense.

steps.title: Chill before cooking
steps.text: Rest the shaped patties on a plate in the fridge for 10 minutes. This firms up the fat so each patty holds its shape in the hot pan instead of slumping, and the cold centre gives the crust time to brown deeply before the middle overcooks.

steps.title: Season just before cooking
steps.text: Season both sides with the salt and pepper only once the patties are ready to go in the pan. Salt left on mince dissolves some of its proteins into a sticky binder, which turns the texture springy and sausage-like instead of loose and tender. If you like, give the tomato slices a tiny pinch of salt as you build.

steps.title: Toast the buns
steps.text: Butter the cut sides of the buns and toast them cut-side down in the pan over medium heat for 1-2 minutes until golden, then set aside. The butter crisps the surface and stops the bread turning soggy once the juicy patty goes in.

steps.title: Get the pan hot
steps.text: Heat the pan over medium-high for 3 minutes, then add 1 teaspoon of oil. A properly hot pan is what builds a deep crust quickly, before the inside has any chance to overcook.

steps.title: Sear the first side
steps.text: Add the patties, 2 at a time or all 4 if your pan is 30cm, and leave them completely untouched for 4 minutes. A deep brown crust should form and the patty should release easily when nudged; this crust is where most of the flavour develops.

steps.title: Flip and melt the cheese
steps.text: Flip each patty just once and cook for a further 3 minutes, adding a slice of cheese for the final 1-1.5 minutes. Cover with a lid or an upturned bowl so the trapped heat melts it evenly. The patties are ready at 71°C in the centre, checked through the side, with clear juices.

steps.title: Rest briefly
steps.text: Lift the patties onto the toasted bun bases and leave for 2 minutes before building. This short rest lets the juices settle back through the meat rather than running out onto the plate.

steps.title: Build the burger
steps.text: Spread ketchup on the bottom bun, then layer lettuce, tomato slices, the cheese-topped patty, red onion rings and pickles, finishing with mustard on the top bun. Building in this order keeps the crisp lettuce next to the bread so it stays fresh rather than going soggy.

tips: Don't press the patties with a spatula while they cook - you'll squeeze out the juices and end up with a dry, flat burger.
Flip each patty only once; constant flipping stops a proper crust forming.
If the pan starts smoking heavily, spoon off a little of the rendered fat rather than lowering the heat, or the patties will steam instead of sear.
Season the mince only just before cooking - salting it early makes the texture springy rather than tender.
storage: Cooked patties keep in a covered container in the fridge for up to 2 days, or frozen without buns or toppings for up to 2 months. Reheat gently until piping hot and reaching 74°C all the way through before eating.
